Chapter 19
Quality Control
Whether for procurement, production, or sales, it’s in a company’s larger
business interest to maintain and improve quality controls across the
entire logistics and supply chain operations.
Quality control involves inspections at all stages, continuous monitoring, and inter-
vening quickly to deal with unexpected events. You can leverage quality control tools
to improve and optimize your business processes. In accordance with ISO 9000, qual-
ity control entails working with techniques and activities that seek to monitor pro-
cesses and remove the causes of unsatisfactory results. To remove these causes,
companies need to undertake corrective and quality-promoting measures that prevent
a defects recurrence. The focus of this chapter will be on supplier evaluation, quality
level, and statistical process control.
This chapter begins with the configuration basics that must be in place to start using
supplier evaluation. Then, it covers the master data that needs to be set up for supplier
evaluation, followed by the business processes and several additional functions that
are available. Next, it covers the quality level and how the system keeps updating infor-
mation over time (and with more data input from business processes). The quality level
works when the dynamic modification rule is in place. The last section delves into cov-
ering statistical process control, control charts, and various other quality control tools
that are available.
To maintain continuity among various sections of this chapter, the transaction and
business data that we use in supplier evaluation business processes eventually leads to
evaluating statistical process control (through control charts).
19.1 Supplier Evaluation
Supplier evaluation makes it easier for the procurement and quality management
functions to pursue their objectives by providing clear and comprehensible key fig-
ures. These objectives include the following:
 Determine the current status of a supply relationship.
 Show the supplier to what extent the requirements of the purchaser are met.
 Create a basis for supplier selection or supplier exclusion.
 Determine support after the request for quotation and extend the supply relationship.

19 Quality Control
826
 Determine support for higher weighting of the goods receipt inspection and inspec-
tion planning.
 Provide background information to conclude a quality assurance agreement.
In supplier evaluation, you use main criteria and subcriteria to establish key figures
that allow an evaluation of individual criteria and the creation of a ranking with an
overall score. Based on these key figures, you can initiate corrective measures and
improvements in a targeted and focused way. A meaningful supplier evaluation isn’t
restricted to determining the current status; instead, it forms the starting point for
ongoing quality improvements.
The supplier evaluation is an essential element of quality control. SAP S/4HANA pro-
vides flexible tools to evaluate your suppliers. All of these tools meet standards
requirements, and you can easily adapt them to meet the business needs of your com-
pany. You’ll learn all the important steps involved in supplier evaluation, but the focus
will remain primarily on quality as one of the criteria that forms an integral part of sup-
plier evaluation.
Supplier evaluation takes an intermediate position between procurement and QM
because it incorporates the information and criteria from both a commercial- and
quality-related point of view. In the SAP S/4HANA system, the supplier evaluation
happens in procurement (materials management [MM]) and evaluates from a com-
mercial point of view, at least in the majority of cases. In addition, the system extracts
master and transaction data from MM, such as material, supplier, and purchasing
information records. The system evaluates the suppliers at the purchasing organiza-
tion level. The purchasing organization is assigned to one or more plants.
Note
During an actual SAP S/4HANA system implementation project, both procurement
(MM) and quality (QM) teams deliberate and agree on the percentages and weighting
by which the criteria and subcriteria will influence supplier evaluation.
The supplier evaluation makes it possible to evaluate each supplier by using a quality
score. The quality score is a combination of all criteria, letting the system create a hit
list (a ranking) of suppliers. You can also consider each criterion in isolation. The sup-
plier evaluation isn’t limited to covering only suppliers of materials but also suppliers
of services, such as maintenance services and cleaning services.
In the following sections, you’ll learn how to configure the criteria and subcriteria,
including assigning a weighting and percentage to each criterion and subcriterion.
Then you’ll maintain the required master data for supplier evaluation, followed by run-
ning end-to-end business processes. In the end, you’ll see how automatic supplier eval-
uation continuously updates the quality score of suppliers.
© 

827
19.1 Supplier Evaluation
19.1.1 Configuration Basics
This section will show you how to make necessary configuration settings that the sys-
tem eventually uses in supplier evaluation.
Weighting Keys
The weighting key is the basic identification to denote equal, different, or unequal weight-
ing of criteria. A criterion is the benchmark, such as price, quality, or on-time delivery,
that you use to evaluate a supplier’s compliance to the company’s business needs.
To navigate to the weighting keys, follow menu path SAP IMG  Materials Management 
Purchasing  Supplier Evaluation  Define Weighing Keys. In the screen that appears,
weighting key 01 denotes equal weighting, whereas weighting key 02 denotes unequal
weighting.
Define Criteria
To evaluate suppliers, the system provides five main criteria and additional subcriteria.
These are the main criteria:
 Quality
 Price
 Delivery
 External service provision
 Service
To navigate to the criteria, use menu path SAP IMG  Materials Management  Purchas-
ing  Supplier Evaluation  Define Criteria. In the screen in Figure 19.1, choose Quality
under Main Criteria and then choose Subcriteria on the left side. This leads to the
screen shown in Figure 19.2.
Figure 19.1 Main Criteria: Overview

Figure 19.2 shows the main criteria 02 (quality) with the following subcriteria:
 GR Inspection
Determination of the quality score from the quality of the inspection lot of the indi-
vidual goods receipts.
 Rejection/Complaint
Determination of the quality score from complaints against suppliers.
 Audit Failure
Determination of the quality score from one or several audits.
Figure 19.2 Evaluation Subcriteria Quality and Scoring Method
Notice the several scoring methods that are available for the subcriteria. Our focus is on
the quality aspects of supplier evaluation, and scoring methods 7, 8, and 9 apply to
goods receipt inspection, shop floor complaints, and audits, respectively. Other scoring
methods apply to quantity reliability, price competitiveness, following shipping
instructions, or timeliness of service delivery (see Figure 19.3).
Tips and Tricks
If you don’t want to use a specific subcriterion for the Quality criteria, then you can
simply leave the Scoring Method field blank (which means No Automatic Determina-
tion; see Figure 19.3).
Tips and Tricks
You can always amend the standard settings to meet the business needs of your com-
pany by adding or removing main criteria or subcriteria as deemed necessary. In total,
up to 99 main criteria and 20 subcriteria per main criteria are possible.

Purchasing Organization Data for Supplier Evaluation
In this step, you maintain the supplier evaluation settings that apply to the entire pur-
chasing organization of the company. To maintain the supplier evaluation data for the
purchasing organization, use menu path SAP IMG  Materials Management  Purchas-

Here, the best score that a supplier can have is 100. The system divides the entire screen
into various areas that apply to different criteria of supplier evaluation.
Let’s evaluate the parameters that are important from a quality perspective for pur-
chasing organization 1710. In the Complaints/Rejection Level area, you can control the
percentage of a supplier’s business volume (ShareBusnVolume%) that impacts the sup-

checkbox, then the system first averages the quality score of all inspection lots and
then makes that average part of supplier evaluation. Other parameters on this screen
pertain to price and on-time delivery.

Tips and Tricks
Remember that a simultaneous use of the Goods Receipt Inspection and Shop Floor
Complaint subcriteria may reduce the quality score twice. The negative, or lower,
usage decision score and the quality notifications created influence the supplier evalu-
ation. Therefore, we recommend using only one of these subcriteria for supplier evalu-
ation, depending on specific business needs.

The quality score calculation is established from the bottom up, which means that you
evaluate the subcriteria first. You determine the quality score of the corresponding
main criteria by combining the subcriteria according to the weighting. Lastly, the sys-
tem reflects the main criteria in the corresponding weighting in the overall score.
Table 19.1 shows an example of how the system calculates and comes to an overall score
after automatic supplier evaluation. Columns 1, 2, 3, and 4 are the ones that you just
configured in the system. Column 5 denotes the quality score that comes from busi-
ness processes such as the usage decision, on-time delivery, or price competitiveness.
Column 6 shows how the system first calculates and subtotals 7 the subcriteria before
moving up to calculate the individual criterion’s totals 8 and then adding up the crite-
ria totals to come up with the overall quality score 9.
Note
Refer to Figure 19.13 to see how these numbers stack up in the SAP S/4HANA system
through automatic supplier evaluation; you achieve an overall quality score of 70.0
here, as shown in in Table 19.1.

Warning
The objective of this chapter is to show you a maximum number of business scenarios
in which quality, as a criterion, influences the supplier evaluation. In reality, don’t
select too many main criteria and subcriteria! A small number of criteria will increase
the level of acceptance and comprehensibility. Start with a simple approach; that is,
use only the Quality criterion with the GR Inspection subcriterion, and make the usage
decision the basis of the quality score.
Let’s now delve into the master data needed for supplier evaluation.
19.1.2 Master Data Maintenance
You need to ensure that the following MM and QM master data exist in the system so
that you can eventually ensure the necessary business processes:
 Business partner master data (Transaction BP)
 Material master record (Transaction MM01)
 Purchasing info record (Transaction ME11)
 Inspection type 01 active in the material master
 Inspection plan for material
 Maintain supplier evaluation (we’ll cover this next)
For this example, use material RM124, supplier EWM17-SU01, plant 1710, and purchasing
organization 1710.
To maintain the weighting key for the supplier evaluation, use Transaction ME61 or fol-
low menu path Logistics  Materials Management  Purchasing  Master Data  Supplier
Evaluation  Maintain. In the initial screen that appears, specify the number of the pur-
chasing organization (1710) and supplier (EWM17-SU01) for which you want to create a
supplier evaluation. This leads to the screen shown in Figure 19.8.
Initially, for a supplier who hasn’t yet been evaluated, the system doesn’t populate the
fields for the main criteria, indicating that it hasn’t determined the quality score yet.
Enter “02” for the Weighting key (for Unequal weighting), and save. Notice that when
you enter “02”, the system brings up the numbers in the Weighting column that you
just configured.
Tips and Tricks
You can use Transaction ME6E for suppliers whose weighing keys aren’t maintained yet.

More  Edit  Auto. New Evaluation in Figure 19.8 (not shown). The system recalculates

19.1.3 Business Processes
You continue to run your business processes as you normally would, and the system
keeps updating the quality score. These business processes may entail creating pur-
chase orders, receiving goods, and performing quality functions such as results record-
ing and usage decision. You also record notifications for defective materials received.
Further, you conduct and record the results and usage decisions of audit inspections in
the system as a part of your routine business.
Note
Refer to Chapter 4 to see how QM integrates with MM, including in the procurement
process. Chapter 12 covers quality notifications, while Chapter 14 has details on audit
inspection.
After you do some or all of the preceding tasks, you can proceed to supplier evaluation.

19.1.5 Additional Functions
There are some additional functions available when you’re already in the supplier evalu-
ation submenu, found at Logistics  Materials Management  Purchasing  Master Data 
Supplier Evaluation. We’ll discuss them briefly in the next sections.
Display Supplier Evaluation
Using Transaction ME62, you can display the supplier evaluation.

Compare Evaluations
Transaction ME64 allows you to determine the quality score of a supplier for a material
or material group and use the quality score for a comparison among all supplied mate-
rials.
Changes
Each new supplier evaluation is also a change to the existing one. Using Transaction
ME6A, you can determine who created a new supplier evaluation and when and there-
fore display the previous as well as current values.
Evaluation in Background
Using Transaction ME6G, you can maintain a job that regularly runs in the background
and, for example, performs a reevaluation of suppliers on a bimonthly basis.
Tips and Tricks
The program name for the background job of supplier reevaluation setup is RM06LBAT,
and you can choose the evaluation frequency, such as weekly or monthly.
Suppliers without Weighting Keys
If you access the automatic evaluation in the background, the weighting key assign-
ment might be missing. An assignment of weighting keys is necessary if you’ve evalu-
ated suppliers with different weighting keys in the background evaluation or haven’t
specified a weighting key. Using Transaction ME6E, you can maintain the background
evaluation with the weighting key.
Print Evaluation Sheet
You can print the document of the current evaluation of a supplier with the overall
score, main criteria, subcriteria, and evaluation. You may often send a printed evalua-
tion sheet to a supplier to inform them about the current status. Prior to this, the
default form generally must be adapted by an SAPscript (ABAP) developer to meet the
company’s requirements. Access the screen in Figure 19.14 using Transaction ME6F to

Some of the key figures available for evaluation are as follows:

Transaction ME6H is available for standard analysis of supplier evaluation.
19.2 Quality Level
The quality level is a data record that contains information on inspection levels for
characteristics, inspection lots, and material, as well as purchasing information of the
supplier. The quality level is relevant only if you’re using the dynamic modification
rule, which determines how you can control a change to the severity of inspections or
in fact skip an inspection. In short, the quality level is a kind of reminder for how the
system should handle the next inspection. For a scheduled dynamic modification, the
system automatically creates a quality level with the next inspection lot. For the first
inspection lot, the system derives the inspection severity from the start level of the

19 Quality Control
842
dynamic modification rule. In the inspection plan of a material, you can make a distinc-
tion between dynamic modification by characteristic and dynamic modification by
inspection lot.
In this section, we’ll discuss some of the options available for the quality level, such as
updating, manually creating, and evaluating the quality level.
19.2.1 Updating the Quality Level during Inspection Lot Creation
If you haven’t maintained the quality level, the system will do it automatically during
inspection lot creation. Initially, the system sets the evaluation to Acceptance and then
increases the relevant counters. Results recording by characteristic has no initial effect
on the evaluation. The evaluation might change with the usage decision. Even if only
one characteristic was rejected (worst-case rule), this leads to a not OK (NOK) evaluation
for a lot-based dynamic modification. Therefore, it’s not the usage decision (e.g., rejec-
tion) that influences the dynamic modification rule, but the rejection of the character-
istic. For a dynamic modification rule by characteristic, the only determining factor is
the evaluation of the particular characteristic.
The usage decision updates the quality level according to the characteristic evalua-
tions. If you make a usage decision without confirming any characteristic results,
which is possible, the dynamic modification rule doesn’t work in the case of a charac-
teristic rejection. The dynamic modification rule can only work as intended if at least
one characteristic is confirmed and completed with a negative result.
Note
Refer to Chapter 3 to learn more about the dynamic modification rule, which you’ll
now use as one of the quality control tools.
19.2.2 Manual Creation of the Quality Level
The system automatically creates a quality level as soon as it triggers the dynamic
modification rule. However, we suggest that you create the quality level manually in
advance because you need to specify a different start level than the one preset in the
dynamic modification rule for certain material. You can create a quality level only for
lot-based dynamic modification. To initially create a quality level, use Transaction
QDL1 or follow menu path Logistics  Quality Management  Quality Inspection  Quality
Level  Create. Enter the necessary details, such as material and plant, and the system
automatically checks whether the dynamic modification rule is already in place. On the
next screen, you can manually set the initial quality level.

19.3 Statistical Process Control
Each business process is subject to dispersion. However, you should have a clear under-
standing of the differences between random dispersion and systematic dispersion:
With random dispersion, small deviations occur constantly, depending on the respec-
tive process parameters, such as tools, operators, and materials. Systematic dispersion,
on the other hand, occurs irregularly and can often be traced to specific influences,
such as temperature, corrosiveness, or a tool’s wear and tear. Random dispersion influ-
ences processes that are already under control.
The entire area of process improvement can be divided into three activities:

19 Quality Control
844
 Process analysis
 Process monitoring
 Process improvement
In process analysis, you monitor the process and then make the required settings by
using statistical methods, including an examination of process capability. If the pro-
cess is stable, you monitor it with methods of statistical process control to eliminate or
reduce existing systematic variances. Next, you optimize the process. To achieve this,
you use statistical process monitoring methods, in which random deviations occur and
you determine what steps or controls you need to take to eliminate these deviations
for process improvement. You need to continue iterating these three activities several
times to continually improve and manage the process.
The following sections will show you how to analyze various data analytics tools avail-
able for statistical process control, including charts, quality scores, and histograms,
among others.
19.3.1 Analyzing Data Using a Control Chart
For process monitoring and improvement, the system offers several methods and
tools:
 Control chart
 Histogram
 Standard distribution
 Run chart
 Ishikawa diagram (cause/effect diagram)
 Pareto chart
 Distribution chart
 Process capability examination
Apart from these quality control charts, the system also supports Six Sigma approaches
for analyzing measured values and nonconformance data, such as Western Electric
rules, capability indicators, trend analysis, and exception analysis. An interface to
external tools (e.g., the QM-STI plug-in) for statistical analysis is also available to allow
you, for example, to verify a significance test.
While evaluating control charts for analysis purposes, a quality chart should help to
answer the following questions:
 Is it a natural process?
 Is there a recognizable trend (increasing or decreasing tendency)?
 Are there systematic or periodic fluctuations?
© 

845
19.3 Statistical Process Control
 Are there jumps in the process?
 Does the process situation change over time?
 Do strong, short-term deviations occur in the control variables?
 Is the process stable (no exceptionally strong fluctuations)?
If control chart analysis or other quality information shows that the process isn’t yield-
ing the desired results, then you need to change the process, or suitable corrective or
preventive actions should be put in place to achieve a stable and controlled process.
19.3.2 Quality Chart
The use of quality control charts forms the basis of statistical process control. Statistical
process control allows you to analyze, monitor, control, and improve processes. Qual-
ity control charts date back to a technique that was developed by Walter A. Shewhart
(1891–1967) in 1924.
In general, you use a control chart to monitor the production process. You can soon
determine whether a process is under control or how changes in processes or para-
meters influence the process. You can also use control charts in the procurement
process—for example, for several goods receipt inspections according to the schedul-
ing agreement with regular releases. In this case, the control chart can indicate whether
the procurement process was under control. In an actual business scenario, the critical
measurement items are set, a sample of the same size is taken at regular intervals, the
control variable is determined by measurement and calculation, and the control vari-
able is entered graphically into the control chart. The typical control variables include
the following:
 Mean value x
 Standard deviations
 Range R
 Median
 Original value
 Number of defective parts
 Number of defects
You can select each control variable as a track for a control chart. If you select two con-
trol variables, you get a dual-track control chart. A typical example of a dual-track con-
trol chart is the x/s control chart (mean value and standard deviation). Depending on
the control chart type, you can set a center line, tolerance, warning, and action limits.
The system calculates the warning and action limits during a preliminary phase under
real process conditions, and they are entered in the control chart.

19 Quality Control
846
The classic types of control charts for quantitative (variable) characteristics include the
following:
 Acceptance chart (e.g., mean-value chart with tolerance)
Focuses on tolerance; gives you upper and lower control and warning limits.
 Shewhart chart (e.g., standard deviation chart)
Uses internal process parameters without considering tolerance limits.
The following are typical control chart types for attributive (countable) characteristics:
 P-chart (fraction)
For defective units.
 Np-chart
For constant sample size.
The lifecycle of a control chart proceeds as follows:
1. Creating the control chart for the first inspection lot
2. Creating the inspection points and recording results
3. Calculating action limits
4. Creating additional inspection lots, inspection points, and inspection results
5. Violation of action limits with quality notifications and SAP Business Workflow
6. Violation of action limits with automatic defects recording
7. Closing the control chart
8. Automatic creation of a control chart for the next inspection lot
The following control chart types are available for inspection characteristics:
 Mean value chart with tolerances (acceptance chart)
 Mean value chart without tolerances (Shewhart chart)
 Standard deviation chart (Shewhart chart)

19.3.4 Process Capability
Figure 19.20 shows the Manage Control Charts app available in SAP S/4HANA with an
overview of various control charts. The top half of the figure is a graphical representa-
tion of various control charts and chart types that were previously discussed in this sec-
tion. The lower half of the screen lists different control charts. As with other SAP Fiori
apps, it’s possible to manipulate the data and information displayed here, as well as set
filters accordingly.
Figure 19.20 Manage Control Charts App
This screen shows the process capability, in which the system determines the mean
value and standard deviation, as well as cp and cpk values, provided that you’ve main-
tained the planned value and tolerance limits for the characteristic. These values are
the process capability indices. The first value (cp) is a measure for the process disper-
sion (is the process controlled?)—that is, how closely a process is running to its specifi-
cation limits relative to the natural variability of the process.
The second value (cpk) describes the position of the mean value in relation to the toler-
ance limits and therefore indicates whether the process is capable. The cpk is an adjust-
ment to the cp affecting its noncentered distribution. In other words, cpk measures
how closely the target values are consistent with normal performance.
For a controlled and capable process, both of these values should be higher than 1.33. In
many industries, the minimum requirement for a process capability index is now 2.0

19.3.5 History of Quality Scores
You learned in Chapter 3 that in the quality inspection business process, a usage deci-
sion is the last step. This is why it’s often referred to as the inspection lot completion
even though the inspection is already completed with the confirmation and comple-
tion of all characteristic results. However, an inspection lot disappears from the work-
list only after you make a usage decision for the inspection lot. In addition to
completing the inspection lot via the usage decision, follow-up functions are automat-
ically or manually triggered or can optionally be initiated. For example, the usage deci-
sion directly influences the supplier evaluation and quality level, and the system also
updates the quality information system. Entering the usage decision code also ensures
that it has a quality score that you defined in the usage decision catalog.

19.3.6 Histogram
Another useful evaluation tool, available in the standard system without any special
settings, is the graphic display of variable measurement values in the form of a histo-
gram. Prerequisites for the use of the histogram are the variable recording of character-
istic results as individual or classed values, as well as the maintenance of tolerance
limits and planned values. Managing a control chart isn’t required for using the histo-
gram. The histogram classification for individual values is calculated through an inter-
nal algorithm. If the inspection results have already been recorded as classed
inspection results, this classification will be used as the histogram basis.
19.4 Summary
In this chapter, you evaluated several quality control tools that weren’t covered in
other chapters. First, you undertook the necessary configuration for supplier evalua-
tion, with a focus on quality as one of the criteria for evaluation. The quality criteria had
three subcriteria—namely, goods receipt inspections, complaints (notifications), and
quality audit. You calculated new scores through automatic supplier evaluation and
then evaluated the additional options available. Then, the quality level required you to
have a working dynamic modification rule already in place. Finally, you gained an
understanding of what it takes to set up and run statistical process control using qual-
ity control charts and the tools they offer to help you improve your quality controls.
